strengths: The paper offers a conceptually clean re-derivation: it shows that the heuristic bidirectional modification of IMF (used in DSBM/ASBM and related methods) is exactly the alternation of IMF projections and IPF projections, thereby giving the previously ad-hoc procedure a principled name (IPMF) and a unifying interpretation. This is a useful clarification for the community.

The theoretical analysis for the Gaussian case is thorough. Theorem 3.1 (characterizing optimality via the matrix Ξ(P,Σ,Σ̃)) and Theorem 3.2 (exponential convergence of parameters, KL divergence, means, covariances, and optimality matrix) are non-trivial, and the appendices contain detailed derivations (Lemmas B.1–B.10, B.5/B.6 for the multidimensional and 1D cases).

The empirical study is reasonably broad: high-dimensional Gaussians (D=128), 2D toy visualization, the SB benchmark with the cBWW2-UVP metric, and real image data (colored MNIST and CelebA), spanning both continuous-time DSBM and discrete-time ASBM implementations.
The paper is generally well organized, the procedure diagrams (Fig. 1) are intuitive, and the code/data sources for DSBM, ASBM and SDE-Edit are referenced, which supports reproducibility.

The demonstration that IPMF can be initialized from arbitrary couplings (e.g., Ind p0 → p0, Inverted 7, SDE-Edit couplings) and still converge is a concrete, empirically-supported insight that goes beyond simply restating existing algorithms.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central claim. The main 'new' result is that the heuristic bidirectional IMF already used in Shi et al. (2023) and Gushchin et al. (2024) equals the composition of IMF and IPF steps. This is a re-interpretation/re-naming of existing algorithms rather than a new algorithm or a new capability that improves on prior SB solvers.

Theoretical contribution is restricted to Gaussians. Theorem 3.2 and all supporting lemmas assume Gaussian marginals and Gaussian starting couplings, with additional conditions on ε, D, and the initial optimality matrix. The claimed general convergence ('General conjecture') is explicitly unproven and is only validated empirically; no partial results (e.g., local convergence, contraction in general settings, or explicit counterexamples where it fails) are provided.

No clear practical improvement. The experiments do not show that IPMF outperforms the existing bidirectional IMF implementations it abstracts; Table 1 shows DSBM-IMF/ASBM-IMF are often similar to or worse than the 'best algorithm on benchmark' row and competitive alternatives, and the FID/MSE plots show different starting processes only trade off fit-to-target versus feature preservation. Thus the framework's practical value beyond interpretability is unclear.

Weak/incomplete baseline comparison. Since the practical algorithm is unchanged from DSBM/ASBM, the paper should either (a) compare against a genuinely different method (e.g., IPF/Sinkhorn-based diffusion SB solvers, SF2M) more thoroughly, or (b) demonstrate a setting where starting from an arbitrary coupling actually helps. Neither is convincingly shown.

The claim of a 'unified framework for solving SB problems' is overstated given the evidence. A genuine unification would require either broader theory (beyond Gaussians) or a demonstration that IPMF can solve problems (e.g., multimodal or real data distributions) where IPF or one-directional IMF fail. The current experiments largely confirm that the existing heuristic works, which was already known.

The paper does not clearly identify the failure modes of IPMF or contrast with cases where standard IMF/IPF are preferable, so the reader does not gain actionable guidance for choosing among the methods.

Presentation issues: the running header 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size' appears throughout (likely a template artifact), and the main text does not always distinguish clearly between claims proven for Gaussians and claims conjectured in general; this could mislead readers about the strength of the theoretical results.
